documents: Shimmoto (2022) JGR Solid Earth 127, e2022JB025157, published PDF (23 pages)
pages_convention: printed journal pages (the article's 'n of 23' numbering, which matches PDF pages counted from 1)

entry.evidence: We need an earthquake source analysis method that does not rely on the simple circular source assumption

steps.action: Poses the problem that a constant kc, which implies a circular symmetric source, may bias stress drops when rupture geometry, speed and directivity vary.
steps.quote: Variations in rupture geometry, speed, and directivity may cause significant errors in the stress drop estimation

steps.action: Takes the author's earlier rectangular bilateral–bidirectional source spectrum model (Shimmoto 2020) as the basis of the spectral ratio method.
steps.quote: The spectral ratio analysis using this source spectrum model enables us to estimate the rupture length, width, speed, and rupture start point.

steps.action: Assembles Hi-net borehole records, F-net and JMA catalogues, and JMA slip inversions for 205 Mw 3.3–5.9 earthquakes in Fukushima and Ibaraki.
steps.quote: I analyzed 205 Mw 3.3–5.9 earthquakes in Fukushima and Ibaraki, Japan

steps.action: Builds the method: multiple-EGF spectral ratio stacks selected by SNR, variance reduction and amplitude-ratio criteria; an envelope-spectrum fit with fc2 and γ constrained; a grid search over prescribed CVS, aspect ratio, Λ and nodal plane; and a 1.05 minimum-residual criterion for uncertainty.
steps.quote: I used spectral ratios stacked for multiple EGFs by station and wave type to improve the stability of the spectral ratios

steps.action: Fits the model to estimate rupture dimensions and computes stress drops ΔσR from the area LW, with variance reductions above 80%.
steps.quote: The stress drops ΔσR are in the range of 5.8–550 MPa with a median of 50.5 MPa

steps.action: Sets the standard source model (square, central nucleation, 0.9 Vs, approximating the circular source) as a rival to the extended model.
steps.quote: It is useful to test if this assumption is generally valid.

steps.action: Compares the standard and extended models with ΔAIC; every event prefers the extended model.
steps.quote: which indicates that all the analyzed earthquakes prefer the extended source model to the standard source model

steps.action: Rejects the standard symmetric model for most events: ruptures are mostly asymmetric, AR = 1 is uncommon and CVS = 0.9 is not favoured.
steps.quote: Thus, the standard source model is less common.

steps.action: Compares ΔσR (10–200 MPa) with the typical 1–10 MPa and with regional differential stress (Yoshida et al. 2015), finding them inconsistent, while they agree with the corner-frequency estimates of Uchide & Imanishi (2016).
steps.quote: The 10–200 MPa stress drops in this study appear inconsistent with the differential stress estimates by Yoshida et al. (2015).

steps.action: Proposes that the fitted area is a smaller, strongly radiating sub-area rather than the overall rupture area.
steps.quote: may not be the overall rupture area but a smaller area that is generating strong seismic radiation

steps.action: Asks what kind of area the spectral ratio method actually estimates.
steps.quote: It is necessary to reveal what kind of area is estimated in the spectral ratio method.

steps.action: Compares the best-fit rupture areas of the two Mw 5.9 events with the JMA finite-fault slip distributions; the estimated areas match the large-slip regions.
steps.quote: The estimated rupture areas from the spectral ratio method seem to correspond to the areas of the large slip regions in the finite fault inversions.

steps.action: Checks the estimated areas and rise times of all events against the Somerville et al. (1999) total-area and largest-asperity scaling regressions; they follow the asperity line.
steps.quote: The rupture areas estimated in this study are consistent with the regression line for the area of the largest asperity

steps.action: Revises the stress drop calculation by treating LW as 17.5% of the total rupture area (Somerville et al. 1999), giving the average static stress drop Δσs.
steps.quote: Since we saw that the estimated rupture area LW is much smaller than the overall rupture area

steps.action: Interprets the source as a single asperity with heterogeneous stress drop, and defines a local stress drop Δσla.
steps.quote: I interpret the results as an earthquake source with a single asperity and heterogeneous stress drop distribution

steps.action: Computes Δσs (0.42–40.2 MPa, median 3.7), Δσla (median 21.1 MPa) and model-dependent uncertainty (median factor 2.45), and finds no depth or spatial trend.
steps.quote: The revised stress drops Δσs range from 0.42 to 40.2 MPa with a median of 3.7 MPa

steps.action: Fits a log-space regression of stress drop on rupture speed (r = −0.53), giving an inverse cube relation, and examines the scaling with seismic moment.
steps.quote: The rupture speed and the stress drop are inversely correlated (Figure 11).

steps.action: Repeats the regression with all source models that meet the residual criterion, weighted per event; the inverse cube relation persists.
steps.quote: I also conducted the regression using all source parameters, not only the best-fit rupture model

steps.action: Computes corner-frequency stress drops on the same data and derives ks: Δσs matches Brune's ks (median 0.41), Δσla matches Madariaga's ks, and ks varies widely between events.
steps.quote: These values are consistent with the ks values by Brune (1970)

steps.action: Relates stress drop uncertainty to the resolution of CVS, AR, Ipq, nodal plane, Λ and observation conditions, and reruns the analysis with γ and fc2 fixed; biases stay below a factor of 2.
steps.quote: the low resolutions of fc2 cannot be the cause of the more than 10 times systematic difference

steps.action: Keeps the average stress drop estimate of 1–20 MPa (median 3.7 MPa), with the estimated area read as the largest asperity.
steps.quote: obtained as 1–20 MPa with a median of 3.7 MPa

steps.action: Varies the assumed asperity-to-total area ratio (12.5% and 22.5%) and reports the factor change in stress drops.
steps.quote: the stress drop estimates systematically change by a factor of 1.46 or 0.60, respectively, which does not alter the conclusions

steps.action: Shows the revised stress drops agree with large-earthquake stress drops and with the regional differential stress, and links the asperity reading to SMGA results (Miyake et al. 2003) and to Meng et al. (2020).
steps.quote: The stress drop estimates are consistent with the differential stress of 2–30 MPa

steps.action: Concludes that source heterogeneity must be considered, in addition to rupture geometry, speed and directivity, when estimating stress drops from spectra.
steps.quote: it is important to consider the heterogeneity of stress drop (or slip) distribution

tree.answer: Yes; 205 events, two of them with independent slip inversions
Survives fixing γ and fc2, varying the area ratio, and weighted regressions; uncertainty about a factor of 2.45
Kept: average static stress drop median 3.7 MPa; fitted area corresponds to the large-slip asperity

end.claim: After correcting for the finding that the spectral-ratio rupture area corresponds to the large-slip asperity rather than the total rupture area, average static stress drops are 0.42–40.2 MPa (median 3.7 MPa, model uncertainty median factor 2.45), with local asperity stress drops 5.7 times larger.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing the spectral-ratio rupture areas of the two Mw 5.9 events with the JMA slip inversions showed the areas match the large-slip regions, which forced the reinterpretation and the revised stress drops.

gates.evidence: Data are archived Hi-net, F-net and JMA records chosen to apply the new method; the asperity hypothesis arose after the high ΔσR values (p. 10). That hypothesis faced a test it could have failed: comparison with independent JMA slip inversions for only two events and with the Somerville scaling for all events (pp. 10-11). The 17.5% area ratio is assumed from the literature, not tested per event (p. 12). Nothing is stated as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Akaike Information Criterion for model comparison
Eshelby inclusion solution relating stress drop to rupture area

novelty_claims.quote: I call the source model estimated by the method originally proposed in this study the extended source model.
However, this problem has been less focused on in the analysis of small-to-moderate earthquakes.

limits: No peer-review file was supplied, so only the final_paper sequence is coded; the acknowledgments thank the editor and reviewers, but which changes they forced is unknown. Sub-claims at other statuses: (1) the fitted area corresponds to the largest asperity is best_explanation, supported by two slip inversions done by JMA (not performed here) and by agreement with an external regression; (2) stress drop is inversely proportional to the cube of rupture speed is regularity_in_range (r = −0.53, Mw 3.3–5.9); (3) median ks = 0.41 for Brune spectra is estimate_with_resolution, with large between-event variability. The 17.5% asperity ratio is assumed uniform across events, so the author cautions that only statistical trends of Δσs, not individual values, should be used. Selection from more than 300 to 205 events (removed for fewer than 24 spectral ratios or poor variance reduction) may bias results; its effect is not reported (inference). The composition coding as capability_first is an inference; the walk also has trace-series features (an anomaly leading to a best explanation).

disagreements.target: Constant kc / circular symmetric source assumption (e.g. Madariaga 1976 model) in corner-frequency stress drop studies
disagreements.support: ΔAIC favours the extended model for every event, and most ruptures are asymmetric with varied aspect ratios and speeds.
disagreements.quote: Figure 6 demonstrates that the circular source assumption is inappropriate for the analyzed earthquakes.

disagreements.target: Uchide and Imanishi (2016) stress drops (4–95 MPa, median 26 MPa)
disagreements.support: Their Madariaga-model stress drops match the local asperity stress drop Δσla rather than the average static stress drop.
disagreements.quote: the stress drops estimated using the Madariaga model by Uchide and Imanishi et al. (2016) are consistent [...]

disagreements.target: Meng et al. (2020) second-moment stress drops in southern California (median 41.8 MPa)
disagreements.support: By analogy with this study's asperity result, their high values may reflect a compact sub-area controlling the characteristic duration.
disagreements.quote: these high-stress drop estimates may imply a small area compared to the total rupture area controls the apparent characteristic duration

disagreements.target: kc from dynamic simulations of uniform stress drop cracks (Madariaga 1976; Kaneko & Shearer 2015) used for total rupture area
disagreements.support: Corner frequency is controlled by the asperity, so these kc values recover the local rather than the average stress drop.
disagreements.quote: obtained by the dynamic simulation of a uniform stress drop crack model may not be appropriate to estimate the total rupture area

disagreements.support: The median ks derived from the Brune spectrum is 0.41, consistent with Ji et al. (2022), with large between-event variability.
disagreements.quote: The median kc value derived from the Brune spectrum model was 0.41 in this study, which is higher than 0.372 by Brune (1970).

disagreements.support: Small earthquakes have heterogeneous slip, so the uniform-slip area must be corrected for heterogeneity.
disagreements.quote: the source model by Shimmoto (2020) does not incorporate slip heterogeneity and can still be too simple to represent a realistic earthquake rupture
